beats.text: She hid in a tiny attic for seven years.

overlays.hook: She hid in a tiny attic *for seven years.*

beats.text: Born enslaved in Edenton, North Carolina, in 1813.
As a girl, she was sent to the household of Dr. James Norcom, who harassed her for years.
In 1835, she ran. He put out a notice for her capture.
She hid in a crawlspace above her grandmother's house. Nine feet long. Three feet high at its highest. She could not stand up.
She bored tiny holes in the wall, and through them, she watched her children grow.
Summer heat. Winter cold. For almost seven years.
In 1842, she finally escaped north, by boat.
In 1861, she told her story in a book, under a false name, Linda Brent.

visual.caption: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, 1861

beats.text: For years, many believed it was a novel. Then historian Jean Fagan Yellin proved Harriet Jacobs wrote it herself.
Seven years in an attic, and she never gave up on freedom.

facts.claim: Placed under Dr. James Norcom, who harassed her for years.
Fled in 1835; runaway notice published (American Beacon, July 1835).
Hid in a crawlspace at the top of her grandmother's house, 9 ft x 7 ft, 3 ft at the highest; could not stand.
Bored small holes in the wall; through them could see her children.
Almost seven years (1835-1842), through heat and cold.
1842 escape north by boat (to Philadelphia, then New York).
Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, 1861, under the pseudonym Linda Brent.
Long treated as a novel (attributed to editor Lydia Maria Child); Jean Fagan Yellin's research (1980s) established Jacobs's authorship.
